prompt: In `10.20.1.0/30 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.1.1`, what does `proto kernel` tell you?
hint: It names who put the line there.

choices.text: The route leads to the kernel of the machine itself
choices.why: It leads out of eth1; `proto` is about origin, not destination.

choices.text: Somebody typed it with ip route
choices.why: A typed route shows no `proto kernel`; the default typed later has none.

choices.text: The kernel added it when the address was set
choices.why: Right. Setting 10.20.1.1/30 on eth1 created the route to 10.20.1.0/30.

choices.text: The route is reserved for the kernel
choices.why: Every packet r1 forwards uses it.

prompt: pc1's ping printed `From 10.20.10.1 icmp_seq=1 Destination Net Unreachable`. Which machine gave up on the packet?
hint: The address at the start of the line.

choices.text: far1, which refused the ping it received
choices.why: far1 never saw it: the packet stopped one hop from pc1.

choices.text: pc1 itself, before the packet was sent
choices.why: A host with no route prints Network is unreachable and names nobody.

choices.text: ra, which had no route back
choices.why: The packet never reached ra; r1 had nowhere to send it.

choices.text: r1, which had no route for it
choices.why: Right. 10.20.10.1 is r1, and it said so in ICMP.

prompt: A route with no `via`, such as `10.20.1.0/30 dev eth1`, exists because r1 has an address on that cable. It is called a ___ route.
hint: The router is plugged straight into that network.

prompt: Match each part of `10.20.1.0/30 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.1.1` to what it says.
hint: Read the table in the section.

pairs.right: The interface a matching packet leaves by
The destination is on that cable itself
The source address for packets r1 sends there itself

right_distractors: The hardware address of r1's port

prompt: What does `default` stand for in `default via 10.20.1.2 dev eth1`?
hint: How many bits does it compare?

choices.text: 0.0.0.0/0, which every address matches
choices.why: Right. Zero bits to compare, so it contains everything.

choices.text: The first route r1 was given
choices.why: Order has nothing to do with it; the connected routes came first.

choices.text: The route to r1's own subnet
choices.why: That is 10.20.10.0/24, a connected route.

choices.text: A route the kernel invents when the table is empty
choices.why: Before it was typed, r1 had no default and said Net Unreachable.

prompt: Only `via 10.20.1.2` was typed, yet the route reads `dev eth1`. How did r1 pick eth1?
hint: Which connected route contains 10.20.1.2?

choices.text: ra told r1 which of its ports to use
choices.why: Nothing was exchanged; r1 worked it out from its own table.

choices.text: eth1 was the first interface on the list
choices.why: eth0 comes first, and position decides nothing.

choices.text: eth1's subnet contains 10.20.1.2
choices.why: Right. A next hop has to be on a directly connected network.

choices.text: ARP found ra on each of r1's ports
choices.why: ARP only asks on the port the table picked.

prompt: How many bits of a destination address does the default route, 0.0.0.0/0, compare?
hint: The number after the slash.

prompt: After r1 got its default, the traceroute from pc1 to 10.30.5.10 completed. What else had to be true for the replies to reach pc1?
hint: A route works in one direction.

choices.text: ra had a route back to pc1's network
choices.why: Right. The lab set it up; without it, far1's answers would stop at ra.

choices.text: pc1 had its own route to 10.30.0.0/16
choices.why: pc1 sends everything to r1 by its default; it needs nothing more.

choices.text: far1 was told the path the request took
choices.why: IP keeps no record of the way a packet came.

choices.text: rb forwarded the replies on ra's behalf
choices.why: rb plays no part in this traceroute.

prompt: r1 holds `10.30.0.0/16 via 10.20.1.2` and `10.30.5.0/24 via 10.20.2.2`. Which way does a packet for 10.30.5.99 leave?
hint: Both routes contain it.

choices.text: Via ra, because the /16 is listed first
choices.why: The order of the list decides nothing.

choices.text: Via rb, by the /24
choices.why: Right: 24 matching bits beat 16.

choices.text: Via ra, because the /16 covers more addresses
choices.why: Covering more is exactly what makes it lose.

choices.text: Split between both, packet by packet
choices.why: One route wins; nothing here shares the load.

prompt: After the /16 and the /24 were added, how many routes in r1's table contain the address 10.30.5.10?
hint: Do not forget the one that contains everything.

prompt: With the table of this section, which destinations does r1 send via rb, 10.20.2.2? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only the /24 points at rb.

choices.why: Right: inside 10.30.5.0/24.
Right: also inside the /24.
Only the /16 contains it, and that is via ra.
The third number is 6: the /16 again, via ra.
Only the default contains it, via ra.

prompt: Suppose the /24 via rb had been typed before the /16 via ra. Which way would 10.30.5.10 leave?
hint: Does the order of typing enter the rule?

choices.text: Via ra, since the /16 was typed last
choices.why: The last route typed has no advantage.

choices.text: Via ra, since the /16 would replace the /24
choices.why: Two different prefixes live side by side.

choices.text: Via the default, since the two would conflict
choices.why: They do not conflict; one contains the other.

choices.text: Via rb, by the /24, exactly as before
choices.why: Right. The length decides, not the order.

prompt: A router holds 10.0.0.0/8, 10.30.0.0/16, 10.30.4.0/22 and a default. How many bits does the winning route for 10.30.6.1 match?
hint: A /22 covers four values of the third number.

prompt: r1 has two defaults: via ra with metric 100 and via rb with metric 200. While both are up, which is used?
hint: A metric is a cost.

choices.text: Via rb, as 200 is higher
choices.why: Higher is more expensive; the cheaper road wins.

choices.text: The one via ra, metric 100
choices.why: Right, as `ip route get 198.51.100.7` answered.

choices.text: Both, one packet each
choices.why: Different metrics mean one preferred route, not a share.

choices.text: The one typed first
choices.why: The order of typing plays no part.

prompt: After the cable to ra was pulled, `ip route get 198.51.100.7` answered via rb. What made the difference?
hint: Read the default via ra in `ip route show default`.

choices.text: ra sent r1 a message saying that it was down
choices.why: No protocol runs here, and ra could not send over a dead cable.

choices.text: The metric of the route via ra rose to 300
choices.why: The metric stayed 100; the route was taken out of the choice.

choices.text: The route via ra was marked `dead linkdown`
choices.why: Right. With eth1 lost, only the metric 200 route was left to choose.

choices.text: Somebody deleted the route via ra
choices.why: It is still listed, with `dead linkdown` beside it.

prompt: ra crashes, but its port towards r1 stays lit. What does r1's kernel do with a packet for 198.51.100.7?
hint: What did the failover in this section react to?

choices.text: Sends it to ra, since the link is still up
choices.why: Right. Nothing r1 can see has changed, so the metric 100 route stays chosen.

choices.text: Sends it to rb, since ra stopped answering it
choices.why: The kernel does not check whether ra answers; it watched the carrier.

choices.text: Drops it and answers Destination Net Unreachable
choices.why: r1 still has two defaults, and one of them looks fine.

choices.text: Sends it both ways at once
choices.why: One route is chosen.

prompt: In FRR's line `K>* 0.0.0.0/0 [0/100] via 10.20.1.2, eth1`, what is the 0 inside the brackets?
hint: The brackets hold two numbers, in a fixed order.

choices.text: The metric
choices.why: The metric is the second number, 100.

choices.text: The administrative distance
choices.why: Right: `[distance/metric]`, and a kernel route has distance 0 in FRR.

choices.text: The route's age in seconds
choices.why: The age is at the end of the line, 00:00:10.

choices.text: The number of hops to 10.20.1.2
choices.why: Nothing here counts hops.

prompt: Match each source of routes to its default administrative distance.
hint: Lower is more trusted.

prompt: FRR holds two static routes to 10.40.0.0/16: via ra at distance 1 and via rb at distance 200. What did `ip route show 10.40.0.0/16` print?
hint: The routing suite keeps candidates; the kernel gets winners.

choices.text: Both routes, with their distances
choices.why: The kernel showed one line; the other stayed in FRR.

choices.text: The route via rb, which was typed last
choices.why: Typing order plays no part; distance does.

choices.text: One route, via 10.20.1.2
choices.why: Right: the distance 1 route, `proto static`.

choices.text: Nothing, because FRR keeps static routes to itself
choices.why: FRR installs its winners in the kernel.

prompt: A router learns 10.50.1.0/24 from RIP (distance 120) and has a static route for 10.50.0.0/16 (distance 1). Which route carries a packet for 10.50.1.7?
hint: Which of the three rules is applied first?

choices.text: The RIP /24: prefix length is decided first
choices.why: Right. The /24 wins on length before trust is asked about.

choices.text: The static /16, since distance 1 beats 120
choices.why: Distance only compares routes to the same prefix.

choices.text: Whichever has the lower metric
choices.why: Metrics from two sources are not compared, and length comes first anyway.

choices.text: Neither: the two conflict and the packet is dropped
choices.why: Nested routes do not conflict.

prompt: A static route given a high distance, so that it waits behind a better route and is installed only when that one goes, is called a ___ static route.
hint: It sits behind the other one, as on water.

prompt: Put the questions a router asks in choosing a route in the order it asks them.
hint: Length, trust, cost.
items: Which of those has the longest prefix?
Among equals, which source has the lowest distance?
Among those, which route has the lowest metric?
trap: Distance before length is the usual slip: a /24 learned from RIP still beats a static /16 for the addresses inside it.

prompt: A table holds 0.0.0.0/0, 172.16.0.0/12, 172.16.0.0/16 and 172.16.32.0/20. What is the prefix length of the route chosen for 172.16.40.9?
hint: A /20 covers sixteen values of the third number.

prompt: Back at the start of the lesson, pc1 got `Destination Net Unreachable` from 10.20.10.1 for 10.30.5.10. Which one command on r1, typed in this lesson, made the ping work?
hint: r1 needed somewhere to send it.

choices.text: ip link set eth1 up
choices.why: eth1 was already up; the table was the problem.

choices.text: ip route add default via 10.20.1.2
choices.why: Right. With a default via ra, the packet had somewhere to go.

choices.text: ip addr add 10.30.5.1/16 dev eth1
choices.why: That would claim far1's network on the wrong cable.

choices.text: ip neigh flush dev eth1
choices.why: The neighbour table was not the problem; the routing table was.

prompt: Match each thing printed in this lesson to what it means.
hint: Each came from a different section.

pairs.right: The interface under the route lost its signal
A router had no route for the destination
Selected by FRR and installed in the kernel
